shortDefinition: A vapor barrier is a sheet of material, usually heavy plastic, that blocks moisture from passing through a floor, wall, or slab. Under a concrete slab it stops ground moisture from wicking up into the home. It protects flooring, framing, and indoor air from damp and mold.
definitionHtml:
A vapor barrier, sometimes called a vapor retarder, is a moisture-blocking layer built into a home's floor, wall, or slab. It is usually a tough polyethylene sheet. Its job is to keep water vapor on one side from moving through to the other. Under a concrete slab it sits between the soil and the concrete. That stops ground moisture from rising through the slab into the finished floor and the air above.

The barrier matters because concrete is porous and soil holds water. That stays true in the desert, after monsoon rains or under yard irrigation. Without a barrier, the moisture wicks up. It can cup wood floors, lift tile, blister coatings, and feed mold under cabinets. A continuous, sealed sheet stops it. The International Residential Code and the Department of Energy both call for a vapor retarder under slabs and in moisture-prone assemblies. Seams get lapped and taped so no gaps remain.

Take a custom home in Casa Grande built on irrigated farmland soil. It gets a heavy under-slab vapor barrier before the concrete is poured. That ground stays damp enough to ruin wood and luxury vinyl flooring over time. Skipping the barrier to save a small material cost is a common and expensive mistake.

A vapor barrier controls moisture. Insulation rated by R-value controls heat. They are separate layers doing different jobs, even when they sit in the same wall or floor. The barrier also has to go on the correct side and stay continuous. Put it on the wrong side and it traps moisture instead of stopping it. We install a sealed under-slab vapor barrier on every foundation, because guarding against ground moisture costs far less than tearing out a damaged floor later.

shortDefinition: A water-resistive barrier (WRB) is a water-shedding layer installed behind a wall's exterior cladding, such as stucco or siding, to keep moisture that gets past the surface from reaching the framing and sheathing. The IRC requires at least one layer on most exterior walls.
definitionHtml:
No exterior finish is perfectly waterproof. Wind-driven rain, sprinkler overspray, and small cracks let some water through stucco, brick, or siding, which is exactly why builders install a water-resistive barrier (WRB), a continuous water-shedding sheet between the wall's outer cladding and the sheathing or framing behind it. The WRB catches that water and drains it back out so the wood structure stays dry. Common materials are asphalt-saturated felt (building paper), Grade D paper used under stucco, and modern house wraps.

The 2021 International Residential Code (IRC), in Section R703, requires a water-resistive barrier behind most exterior wall coverings. Behind stucco, the code calls for the equivalent of two layers of Grade D paper, because wet stucco bonds to and can compromise a single layer as it cures. The barrier laps shingle-style, each upper piece over the one below, so gravity carries water down and out rather than behind the layer.

In Arizona, most production and custom homes wear three-coat stucco, so the WRB lives behind that stucco and ties into the weep screed at the bottom of the wall, which lets the drained water escape. During monsoon season, that drainage path is what keeps a wind-driven downpour from soaking the wall framing.

A WRB is not the same as a vapor barrier. A WRB blocks liquid water from the outside while still letting the wall dry; a vapor barrier controls water vapor moving through the assembly. Both manage moisture, but they sit in different places and solve different problems. Getting the WRB lapped and flashed correctly at windows and the base of the wall is one of the most important defects-prevention steps in the whole exterior.

seoTitle: Weep Screed for Stucco: What It Does and IRC Height Rules
shortDefinition: A weep screed is a metal trim strip installed at the base of a stucco wall that gives trapped water a path to drain out and stops the stucco short of the soil. The IRC sets a minimum height: at least 4 inches above grade or 2 inches above paved surfaces.
definitionHtml:
Right where a stucco wall meets the foundation, a long L-shaped or J-shaped metal strip called a weep screed gets nailed along the bottom edge. It does two jobs. It gives the stucco a clean, straight stopping point above the ground, and it lets any water that drained down behind the stucco escape through small weep holes in its bottom flange instead of pooling inside the wall.

The 2021 International Residential Code (IRC), Section R703.7.2.1, requires a weep screed at the base of exterior stucco walls on framed construction. The code sets a minimum height: the screed must sit at least 4 inches above the earth (grade) or at least 2 inches above paved surfaces like a sidewalk or patio. The water-resistive barrier and the stucco lap over the top flange of the screed so water is directed onto and out through it.

In Arizona, weep screed placement is a common point of trouble because of how homes meet the desert. When landscapers later raise the soil, pour a patio, or bank gravel against the wall and bury the weep screed, the drainage path is blocked and stucco can wick moisture from the ground. That trapped moisture leads to staining, efflorescence, and rot, and a buried weep screed is a frequent construction defect complaint.

A weep screed is different from other stucco trims like casing bead or control joints, which shape edges and manage cracking rather than drain water. The rule to remember on any Arizona home: keep soil, mulch, and hardscape below the weep screed so it can do its one job, which is to let the wall drain.

shortDefinition: Backflow prevention is the device or assembly that stops used or contaminated water from flowing backward into a home's drinking water. It goes at every point where a clean pipe could meet a dirty one, such as a hose bibb, an irrigation line, a pool fill valve, or a storage tank.
definitionHtml:
The spot you are guarding is called a cross-connection: any place a potable water line can touch water that is not safe to drink. Backflow is that water traveling the wrong way. It happens two ways. Backsiphonage is a pressure drop, say a main breaks down the street, pulling water backward like a straw. Backpressure is something downstream, usually a pump, pushing harder than the city main.

The hardware that breaks the path is ranked by how much it protects. An air gap is the strongest, an open vertical space at least twice the width of the outlet opening, because air cannot siphon. Below it sit a reduced pressure assembly, a pressure vacuum breaker set at least 12 inches above the highest pipe downstream, and an atmospheric vacuum breaker set at least 6 inches above.

A desert lot piles these up fast. The plumbing code puts a vacuum breaker on every sillcock and hose bibb, and a vacuum breaker or reduced pressure assembly on yard irrigation. Inject fertilizer through that irrigation and the code steps you up to the reduced pressure assembly. Add a pool auto-fill valve, an evaporative cooler makeup line, and on unserved land a cistern topped off by hauled water, and one house carries half a dozen.

Here is the part owners get backward. Arizona's cross-connection rule, A.A.C. R18-4-215, is what makes a water utility require and yearly test these assemblies. It exempts single-family homes used only as residences, unless a cross-connection problem turns up. So on a normal custom home the plumbing code drives the devices, and your plumbing inspection is where they get checked.

For example, a Scottsdale build with a zoned drip system gets a pressure vacuum breaker about a foot above the highest emitter. Under the state rule that device only holds up on irrigation with no chemicals and no backpressure. Start running fertilizer through it and it has to become a reduced pressure assembly.

seoTitle: Bonding Jumper: What It Is and Where Code Requires It
shortDefinition: A bonding jumper is a conductor that ties separate metal parts together so they all sit at the same voltage. The main bonding jumper does this once, at the electrical service, joining the neutral to the metal enclosure. Other jumpers bond items like gas piping to the same ground.
definitionHtml:
Grounding and bonding get used as one word on a job site, but they do different jobs. Grounding connects the system to the earth. Bonding ties metal parts to each other so none of them can float at a different voltage than its neighbor. A bonding jumper is the piece of wire or strap that does the tying. Get it wrong and the metal in your house can sit quietly energized instead of tripping a breaker.

The one that matters most is the main bonding jumper, covered by Section E3607.5 of the 2021 International Residential Code. It is unspliced, it lives inside the service enclosure, and it connects the neutral to the metal box and the equipment grounding wires. That bond gets made once. Past the service, every subpanel keeps neutral and ground on separate bars, which is why a detached casita or shop is fed with a four-wire feeder instead of three.

Equipment bonding jumpers are the second family, and they show up wherever metal could become energized. Gas piping is the common one. Pinal County states it plainly in its residential gas bulletin: any above-ground gas piping that can become energized has to be bonded to the electrical service electrode system, and a system containing CSST needs a jumper no smaller than 6 AWG copper, run no more than 75 feet.

For example, a Cave Creek custom home with a propane range gets both. The electrician makes the main bond in the service panel at rough-in. Then a 6 AWG copper jumper runs from the steel gas pipe past the second-stage regulator back to the ground at the service. Two jumpers, two purposes, and on most jobs two different trades. The main bond is an electrician's item all day. The gas jumper is the one that falls through the crack, because the plumber sets the pipe and the electrician lands the wire.

shortDefinition: Ceiling height is the clear distance from the finished floor to the finished ceiling. The building code sets a minimum of 7 feet for habitable rooms and hallways, and 6 feet 8 inches for bathrooms, toilet rooms, and laundry rooms, with separate rules for sloped ceilings and dropped beams.
definitionHtml:
Section R305 of the International Residential Code sets the floor. Habitable space, hallways, and the parts of a basement holding them need a ceiling of at least 7 feet, measured finished floor to finished ceiling. Finished means after drywall and flooring go in, not at framing. Bathrooms, toilet rooms, and laundry rooms may drop to 6 feet 8 inches.

The exceptions do the real work. Sloped ceilings get measured differently: at least half of the room's required floor area has to reach 7 feet, and floor with less than 5 feet of headroom does not count toward that required area at all. That single rule is what makes lofts, dormers, and rooms tucked under a roof buildable. Beams, girders, and ducts are allowed to hang below the ceiling line, and in a basement with living space the 2021 IRC lets them come down to 6 feet 4 inches. Above a shower or tub, the height only has to leave the fixture usable.

The 7 foot minimum almost never binds on an Arizona custom home. Standard plate height across the Valley is 9 or 10 feet, and great rooms often run 12 feet or higher, partly for proportion and partly because tall volume carries hot air up away from where you sit. Where R305 actually gets tested is at the obstructions.

For example, on a Scottsdale great room with an exposed beam, the designer can drop that beam for looks right up to the point where it eats the required headroom. Push past it and the correction happens at framing, with the beam already set. The same math governs a stair soffit over a hallway and a bulkhead hiding a duct run to a rear bedroom. Catch those heights during plan review, while they are still lines on paper.

shortDefinition: A condenser pad is the base that an outdoor air conditioner or heat pump sits on. The residential code requires ground-supported equipment to be level and firmly set on concrete or another approved material that rises at least 3 inches above the surrounding dirt, with room left around it for service.
definitionHtml:
Most condenser pads are precast concrete, a poured slab, or a molded composite tray. They carry the outdoor half of the system: the compressor, the condenser coil, and the fan. The pad is not decoration. Section M1305.1.3.1 of the International Residential Code sets three conditions for equipment supported from the ground. It has to be level. It has to sit firmly on a concrete slab or other approved material that extends not less than 3 inches above the adjoining ground. And it goes in the way the manufacturer directs.

Clearance is the other half of the rule. Section M1305.1 calls for a level working space at least 30 inches deep and 30 inches wide in front of the control side. The unit also has to stay reachable for service without tearing out permanent construction. Landscaping added later is what usually breaks this, when a block wall or a hedge closes in on equipment that passed inspection years earlier.

For example, an outdoor unit set straight onto decomposed granite in a Rio Verde yard sits down in the dust line. Blowing dust and fine gravel pack the coil fins. Monsoon runoff and drip irrigation pool under the cabinet. The unit slowly goes out of level as the soil moves. A pad lifts the coil above all of that, lets stormwater pass underneath, and gives the installer a solid base to fasten the unit to.

Set the pad right the first time, because moving one later means breaking into refrigerant lines. Size it so the unit sits fully on the pad with no overhang. Keep it out from under a roof drip line. Put it where a technician can open the service panel and stand in front of it. On expansive soil, ask the HVAC contractor to bed the pad on compacted base rather than loose backfill, so it does not tip a season after the pour.

shortDefinition: CSST is corrugated stainless steel tubing, the flexible yellow or black gas line used in most new homes in place of rigid black iron pipe. Its wall is thin, so code requires yellow CSST to be bonded to the home's electrical grounding system with a copper jumper.
definitionHtml:
Corrugated stainless steel tubing comes on a reel and bends around framing, so a plumber runs one length from the gas manifold to an appliance. Rigid black iron has to be cut, threaded, and fitted at every turn. That speed is why CSST sits behind the drywall of most new Arizona homes. The trade-off is the wall. CSST is thin where black iron is heavy, and that thinness drives the one extra rule it carries.

Section G2411 of the 2021 International Residential Code requires yellow CSST to be bonded straight to the home's grounding electrode system. The bonding jumper is 6 AWG copper at a minimum and can run no more than 75 feet from the gas pipe to the ground connection. The clamp lands on a metal pipe, a pipe fitting, or a brass CSST fitting. It never grips the corrugated tubing itself.

Lightning is the reason, which is what makes the rule earn its keep in an Arizona monsoon. A strike near the house pushes a large voltage onto every metal system inside. If the gas tubing sits at a different voltage than a nearby duct or water line, the difference can arc across the gap, burn a pinhole through the thin CSST wall, and light the gas behind it. Bonding puts both on the same ground, so no gap is left to jump.

For example, Pinal County writes the rule into its own gas piping bulletin: a system containing CSST needs a jumper no smaller than 6 AWG copper. On natural gas the jumper lands downstream of the meter. On a propane lot near Rio Verde it lands past the second-stage regulator. Black arc-resistant CSST is built to take the hit and gets treated differently, but splice in one piece of yellow tubing and the bond comes back. The trap on a real job is that the plumber sets the tubing and the electrician lands the bond, so put that connection on somebody's scope in writing.

shortDefinition: A defrost cycle is the short stretch when a heat pump reverses itself to melt frost off the outdoor coil. In heating mode that coil runs colder than the outside air, so moisture freezes onto it and chokes airflow. The unit briefly runs in cooling mode until the coil clears, then returns to heating.
definitionHtml:
Frost on a heat pump is physics, not a fault. When the unit heats your house, it is pulling warmth out of the outdoor air, which leaves the outdoor coil running well below the temperature around it. Any moisture in that air can freeze onto the fins. A layer of ice blocks airflow across the coil and heating capacity falls off quickly, so the controls stop heating and clear it.

The fix is a brief role reversal. A reversing valve flips the refrigerant flow so the outdoor coil turns hot and melts its own ice, and the outdoor fan is held off while that happens. Because the indoor coil is now the cold one, many systems switch on electric strip heat at the same time so your registers do not blow cool air. The cycle ends when the coil sensor reads about 57 degrees, usually after 30 seconds to a few minutes.

For example, a Rio Verde owner might step outside on a January morning and see steam pouring off the outdoor unit. That is a normal defrost, not a breakdown. It is also uncommon here. Frost needs cold and moisture together, and the low desert supplies neither in quantity. Phoenix's normal January low sits in the low to mid 40s, and winter air is dry. Cave Creek and Apache Junction run colder than Sky Harbor, but nothing close to a Midwest winter.

That is a real argument for heat pumps in Arizona. In a cold, damp climate a unit can defrost several times an hour, burning backup electric heat each time and dragging its seasonal heating efficiency down. Here the penalty is close to noise, which is one reason a single heat pump handles both jobs on most new custom homes. If you do see the outdoor unit icing over again and again, or ice stacking on top of the cabinet, the defrost control or its sensor has usually failed. That is a service call, not weather.

shortDefinition: Drainage is how storm water moves across a lot and leaves it. On an Arizona build it covers the finished grade, the swales, and the path monsoon runoff takes around the house. Code requires the ground to fall at least 6 inches in the first 10 feet away from the foundation.
definitionHtml:
Site drainage is the shape of your ground and the route water takes over it. It is a separate thing from the drain lines inside the house. This is the outdoor version: the finished grade, the swales, the driveway crown, and where a monsoon storm sends water once it comes off your roof.

The base rule lives in the foundation chapter of the residential code. Lots have to be graded so surface water runs away from the foundation walls, and the grade must fall at least 6 inches within the first 10 feet. Where a property line, a wall, or a slope blocks that, you build swales or drains instead, and hard surfaces within 10 feet slope at least 2 percent away.

Arizona adds its own problem. Desert storms arrive fast and sheet across flat ground rather than running in a channel, and the caliche and tight clay under many Valley lots absorb little of it. So the plan has to carry runoff around the home and off the property without pushing it onto the neighbor. That last part is the correction that costs the most to fix later.

Drainage is a permit, not only a detail. In unincorporated Maricopa County, the drainage review uses a grading matrix to estimate how much engineering your plan needs. Paradise Valley is tighter: add 999 square feet of hard surface, or price the work above $500,000, and a grading and drainage plan attaches to the house permit, signed by an Arizona registered civil engineer along with the survey and the stormwater plan.

For example, on a Rio Verde Foothills parcel with a wash across one corner, the engineer sets the pad clear of the flow path and shapes a swale to route storm water around the home. One thing owners miss: that 6-inch fall has to survive the landscaper. Check the finished grade again after the yard goes in.

seoTitle: Egress: Bedroom Window and Door Rules Explained
shortDefinition: Egress is the way out of a building in an emergency. In a house it covers two paths: the normal route of doors, hallways, and stairs to the outside, and the emergency escape and rescue opening, usually a window, that every bedroom, basement, and habitable attic must have.
definitionHtml:
Fire is why egress exists as a code word. The International Residential Code splits it in two. Section R311 covers the everyday way out: one side-hinged exterior door, hallways at least 36 inches wide, stairs you can take fast in the dark. Section R310 covers the backup route, and that is the half that actually shapes a custom home.

Every sleeping room, every basement, and every habitable attic needs at least one operable emergency escape and rescue opening. Almost always that means a window. The 2021 IRC pins it to four numbers, all measured with the window opened the normal way from inside: a net clear opening of at least 5.7 square feet, at least 24 inches of clear height, at least 20 inches of clear width, and a sill no higher than 44 inches above the finished floor. An opening on the grade floor may drop to 5 square feet. Net clear means the hole a body fits through, not the rough opening the framer cut.

Those numbers fight each other on purpose. Twenty-four inches by twenty inches is only 3.3 square feet, so one dimension has to grow well past its minimum.

For example, a single-hung window opens only half its height, so a Fountain Hills bedroom needs a tall enough unit that the open half still clears 24 inches. Casements pass more easily, because the whole sash swings out. The 44 inch sill then collides with things Valley buyers ask for: deep window seats, floor-to-ceiling glass walls, platform beds. Tag the egress units on your window schedule so the framer sets the right rough opening the first time. Inspectors check egress at framing and again at the final inspection, and a bedroom window moved after stucco is a real bill.

shortDefinition: An energy storage system, or ESS, is a stationary home battery that stores electricity for later, usually charged by rooftop solar or cheap off-peak power. Building code treats it as fire equipment rather than an appliance, so it has to be listed to UL 9540 and it can only go in certain places.
definitionHtml:
A home energy storage system is a battery cabinet rated in kilowatt-hours, wired between your solar array, your panel, and the utility. A Tesla Powerwall or an Enphase IQ Battery is the version most Arizona owners know. It charges while the sun is up or rates are low, then carries the house through an outage or the pricey hours of a time-of-use plan.

Section R328 of the International Residential Code governs the install. It is new in the 2021 edition. The battery has to be listed and labeled to UL 9540. UL caps a single unit at 20 kilowatt-hours. Indoors, in a utility closet, basement, or storage space, the total is 40 kilowatt-hours. In a garage, on an exterior wall, or outdoors, the total is 80. Units sit at least 3 feet apart, unless a UL 9540A fire test documents a shorter distance.

Where it can go is what shapes the design. R328.4 allows four spots. Detached garages and accessory structures. Attached garages separated from the living space. An exterior wall or outdoor spot, at least 3 feet from any door or window into the house. And enclosed utility, storage, or basement rooms with finished or noncombustible walls, where unfinished wood framing gets 5/8 inch Type X gypsum board. Then a hard line: an ESS shall not go in sleeping rooms, or in closets or spaces opening directly into sleeping rooms.

For example, a Fountain Hills home pairs two 13.5 kilowatt-hour batteries with rooftop solar, almost always on a garage wall. R328.4 keeps them out of the living space, and a garage clears both caps. Pick that wall carefully. Every battery publishes an operating temperature range, and an unshaded west wall in Phoenix is the hottest surface on the lot in July. One local wrinkle: R328 did not exist in the 2018 IRC. If your AHJ still enforces that edition, the electrical code, NFPA 855, and the maker's instructions govern instead.

shortDefinition: An evaporative cooler, commonly called a swamp cooler, cools a home by pulling hot outside air through water-soaked pads. Evaporation absorbs heat, so the air leaving the pads is much cooler. It performs well in dry desert air and loses much of that power once monsoon humidity arrives.
definitionHtml:
A fan, a small water pump, and a set of thick fibrous pads are the whole machine. The pump keeps the pads wet, the fan pulls outside air through them, and water evaporating off those pads takes heat out of the air. How far the temperature drops depends on how dry the incoming air already is, which engineers measure as wet-bulb temperature. Dry air carries more cooling potential, so the same unit behaves very differently in June than it does in August.

Section M1413.1 of the International Residential Code sets the install rules. The equipment has to be listed, and it goes in per the manufacturer's instructions, on a level platform a technician can reach for service, with any opening through an exterior wall flashed against water. Two more conditions matter here. The water line feeding the pads must be protected so cooler water can never siphon back into your drinking water, and the air intake has to sit away from plumbing vents and flues.

For example, a Cave Creek home with a rooftop down-draft cooler runs cheaply through the dry heat of May and June, then fades in July. Arizona's monsoon drives dew points up, and moist air cannot absorb much more water, so the pads stop delivering. That seasonal cliff is why most custom homes here treat evaporative cooling as a shoulder-season system and run a heat pump for the rest of the year.

A swamp cooler is not a cheaper air conditioner. It adds moisture instead of removing it, and it works on a single pass of outside air, so a window or a relief vent has to stay open to let that air back out. Refrigerated air recirculates and dries. Upkeep differs too: pads, float valve, and pump get serviced every spring, and the water line gets drained every fall so nothing sits standing in it.

shortDefinition: Flame spread index is a number that rates how quickly fire travels across the surface of a building material. It comes from the ASTM E84 tunnel test, where fiber-cement board scores 0 and red oak flooring scores 100. Codes use the score to decide where a material is allowed to be used.
definitionHtml:
The number comes out of one specific test. In ASTM E84, also published as UL 723 and known as the Steiner tunnel test, a sample about 24 feet long is mounted face down in the ceiling of a tunnel. A gas flame burns at one end for 10 minutes while technicians track how far fire travels. Results are scaled against two reference materials: fiber-cement board is 0, select-grade red oak flooring is 100. The same run yields a smoke-developed index, which scores how much smoke it puts out.

Codes sort that raw number into groups. Under Section 803.1.2 of the International Building Code, interior wall and ceiling finishes are Class A at 0 to 25, Class B at 26 to 75, and Class C at 76 to 200, and all three cap smoke-developed index at 450. The residential code sets a ceiling instead of a class: Section R302.9.1 caps wall and ceiling finishes at a flame spread index of 200, and R302.9.2 caps smoke at 450.

For example, a Scottsdale great room with a tongue-and-groove wood ceiling is where the number bites. Most untreated softwoods land in the Class B or Class C range, which clears R302.9.1 for a ceiling finish in a house. Fire-retardant treatment moves the same species into Class A, which a stricter assembly or local amendment may require. Ask the supplier for the ASTM E84 report before you spec the material, not after.

Insulation carries a tighter limit. Section R316.3 requires foam plastic in a home to test at a flame spread index of 75 or less, and a smoke-developed index of 450 or less, measured at the thickness you plan to install. Passing that test does not let the foam stay exposed. It still sits behind a thermal barrier. Flame spread rates how a surface burns; a thermal barrier keeps fire off the foam to begin with.

shortDefinition: A floodplain is land that a mapped flood is expected to cover. FEMA draws the line at the base flood, the flood with a 1 percent chance of happening in any given year. In Arizona, building inside one means a raised finished floor, a separate floodplain permit, and a lender asking about flood insurance.
definitionHtml:
The regulated version of a floodplain is the area of special flood hazard: land subject to a 1 percent or greater chance of flooding in any given year. FEMA maps it, and the flood it maps is the base flood. Arizona's version is rarely a river. It is a dry wash that runs hard for an hour, or flat desert that floods as sheet flow, which federal rules call an area of shallow flooding, 1 to 3 feet deep on average.

Building there takes a second approval. Under A.R.S. 48-3613, no development may occur in a delineated floodplain without written authorization from the flood control district board, and development covers grading, filling, and paving, not only the house itself. In the Phoenix metro that board is the Flood Control District of Maricopa County, which writes and enforces the floodplain regulations for the unincorporated county and 14 cities and towns. Its floodplain use permit asks for a site plan, an engineer's report, and your finished floor elevations.

Height is where the money goes. The lowest floor has to sit at or above the design flood elevation, and most communities add freeboard, a safety margin in feet above the flood level. Section R322 of the residential code then calls for flood-damage-resistant materials below that line and puts the electrical, HVAC, and plumbing equipment above it.

For example, take a five-acre Rio Verde Foothills parcel with a wash across one corner. The pad moves out of the flow path, the finished floor gets raised, and the floodplain use permit adds fees and staff review on top of the building permit. The flag follows you into other permits too. A rooftop solar array on a floodplain parcel loses access to Maricopa County's faster SolarAPP+ review path.

A floodplain lot is still buildable. Pull the flood status during due diligence, before you buy, because the finished floor elevation drives the foundation, the driveway, and the price.

shortDefinition: A grounding electrode system is the set of metal parts that connect a home's electrical system to the earth, all bonded together into one path. It can include a concrete-encased electrode cast into the foundation, a driven ground rod, a buried metal water pipe, a ground ring, or a plate.
definitionHtml:
A ground fault or a lightning surge has to go somewhere, and the earth is where it goes. The grounding electrode system is how your house reaches the dirt. Section E3608 of the 2021 International Residential Code lists what counts as an electrode and adds one firm rule: every electrode present at the building gets bonded together into a single system, not left as separate paths.

Five things qualify. A buried metal water pipe touching soil for 10 feet or more. A concrete-encased electrode, meaning 20 feet of half-inch rebar or 20 feet of 4 AWG bare copper cast into a footing under at least 2 inches of concrete. A ground ring. A driven rod or pipe at least 8 feet long. A buried metal plate. Whichever exist at your house have to be tied together.

Arizona is where the concrete-encased electrode was invented, and the reason is the dirt. Herbert Ufer solved this for the U.S. Army in 1942 while building bomb storage vaults near Tucson and Flagstaff, where the dry, sandy ground read too high for driven rods to work. Concrete holds moisture and spreads contact over a wide surface, so a properly built Ufer holds around four ohms for the life of the foundation.

For example, a rural build in Rio Verde on hauled water has no metal water main to use, so the list gets shorter before the electrician starts. The code also requires a second electrode alongside a lone driven rod unless that rod tests at 25 ohms or less, and in caliche and rock that reading is hard to hit. So the Ufer carries the job and a rod backs it up, spaced at least 6 feet from any other rod. The practical part for an owner: the rebar gets tied and the connection set before the footing pour, and nobody can add it later.

shortDefinition: A habitable attic is attic space finished as a real room, not storage. Building code treats it as living space, so it needs minimum floor area, a 7 foot ceiling over at least half that area, an emergency escape window, and a fixed stair instead of a pull-down ladder.
definitionHtml:
Storage attics and habitable attics are two different things to a building inspector. A habitable attic is finished attic space people use as a room: a loft, a bonus room, a bedroom under the roof. Section R326 of the International Residential Code sets what it takes to get there. The space needs the same minimum floor area as any other room, at least 70 square feet, plus a ceiling height that follows the normal room rules.

Because the roof slopes, that height gets measured a specific way. At least half of the required floor area has to stand 7 feet or taller, and floor with less than 5 feet of headroom does not count toward the required area at all. Knee walls at the edges are fine as long as the middle of the room carries the height. R326 also holds the occupiable floor area to one third of the story below, or one half in a sprinklered house. Cross that line and the attic counts as another story, which pulls in more code.

The attic also needs its own emergency escape and rescue opening, the same egress window a bedroom needs, plus a fixed stairway. A pull-down ladder does not qualify.

For example, a Cave Creek home can frame a bonus room inside the roof over the garage, with a dormer that lifts 7 feet of ceiling over half the floor and holds the egress window. Standard roof trusses fill the attic with webbing and leave no clear span, so attic trusses or stick framing have to be specified before the roof package is ordered. Decide you want the room after the trusses arrive and you buy them twice.

Do not confuse this with a conditioned attic, which is an insulation detail at the roofline that pulls ductwork into cooled air. That is an energy choice about an attic nobody lives in. An Arizona habitable attic usually needs both, because a room under a Phoenix roof bakes without one.

Sources

shortDefinition: A manometer is the gauge used to read gas pressure, either a U-shaped tube of liquid or a digital meter. A plumber uses one to prove a new gas line holds pressure during the required test, and later to check the pressure feeding an appliance once the gas is turned on.
definitionHtml:
The original manometer is a clear U-shaped tube half full of water. Pressure on one side pushes the column down and up the other, and you read the difference in inches. That is where the unit inches of water column, written in. w.c., comes from. It is a small unit on purpose, since one psi equals about 27.7 inches of water column and house gas runs at a fraction of a psi. Most crews now carry a digital version, but the unit and the idea did not change.

Section G2417.4 of the 2021 International Residential Code names the tool. Test pressure gets measured with a manometer or another device calibrated to show a pressure loss from leakage during the test. The same section caps the gauge: the top of its scale can be no more than five times the test pressure. A 3 psi test therefore tops out at a 15 psi gauge.

That cap is the whole point of the reading. Put a 100 psi gauge on a 3 psi test and a real leak moves the needle a hair, which reads as a pass. Sized right, a leak is obvious. Passing means the number does not move at all across the full hold. Any drop is a leak, and the code answer is to replace the bad section rather than chase it with dope.

For example, Pinal County requires a 10 psi test on a gauge no larger than 30 psi, held and watched by the inspector for at least 10 minutes, with the system already under pressure when he pulls up. One Arizona wrinkle to plan around: air in a sealed pipe gains pressure as it warms and loses it as it cools. A line pumped up in cool morning air and read at noon in Phoenix sun will drift, so set the gauge in shade and let the pipe settle before you call the reading.

shortDefinition: Photovoltaic, shortened to PV, means turning sunlight straight into electricity. A PV panel makes direct current, and an inverter converts it to the alternating current a house runs on. On an Arizona custom home, the array carries its own permit and its own review, filed alongside the house.
definitionHtml:
Photovoltaic names an effect, not a product. A semiconductor cell releases electrons when light hits it, and that flow is direct current. Wire cells into a module, modules into strings, run the output through an inverter, and you get the alternating current your panel feeds. So when a builder's contract says solar, ask which kind. PV makes power. A solar thermal collector only heats water.

What limits an Arizona array is roof geometry and firefighter access, not sunlight. Scottsdale publishes placement guidelines that decide your review lane: panels at least 3 feet below the ridge, two 3-foot-wide access pathways from eave to ridge on each roof slope, and 18 inches off a hip or valley where panels sit on both sides. Meet all three and the permit gets a fast small-scope review. Miss one, or go ground-mounted, and the same house lands in full plan review.

Height and tilt work the same way. On a south-facing pitched roof, the top of the panels stays within 8 inches of the roof surface. On a north, east, or west facing roof, tilt stays under 15 degrees and height under 24 inches. On a low-slope roof, 30 inches. An array with dead loads over 50 pounds at the mounting points needs a structural analysis.

The array is its own permit next to the house permit. In unincorporated Maricopa County a rooftop system files as a minor residential electrical permit, and the county's automated code check, SolarAPP+, does not stand in for it: "This step does not issue a building permit."

For example, an owner tilts a west-facing array to 20 degrees to chase winter production, breaks both the 15-degree and the 24-inch limit, and trades a quick review for a full one. If an HOA is the obstacle instead, A.R.S. 33-1816 bars it from banning a solar device outright, and any placement rule it writes cannot raise your cost or cut the system's output.

shortDefinition: A pool barrier is the wall, fence, and gate system that has to enclose a swimming pool. Arizona law sets the floor at 5 feet measured on the outside, with no opening a 4-inch ball can pass and nothing climbable on the outer face. That is taller than the model code.
definitionHtml:
What governs a pool barrier in Arizona is a state statute, not a building code. A.R.S. 36-1681 reaches any contained body of water 18 inches or more deep at any point and wider than 8 feet at any point that is meant for swimming, so a spa or a large water feature can trigger it along with a pool.

The dimensions are exact. The barrier stands at least 5 feet tall, measured on the exterior side, the face turned away from the water. No opening may pass a 4-inch sphere. Wire mesh or chain link is capped at a 1.75-inch mesh measured horizontally. The outside face cannot carry openings, handholds, or footholds a child could climb, and the barrier has to sit at least 20 inches back from the water's edge. An above-ground pool counts as its own barrier only if its sides are non-climbable and at least 4 feet high, with a removable or secured ladder.

That 5-foot number is where Arizona parts ways with the model code. The International Swimming Pool and Spa Code, which the residential code points to for pools, sets its barrier at 48 inches. Arizona's statute sets 60 and applies statewide, whether or not your city ever adopted a pool code. Where the two differ, the statute governs. A city or county may go stricter, never lower.

For example, on unincorporated Maricopa County land the county puts the top of the barrier at 60 inches above finished grade on the exterior side, and the barrier permit has to be issued before you install the fence, plaster the pool, or add water. That timing is the trap. A barrier is not a punch-list item.

The statute exempts a residence where every resident is at least six years old, along with pools built before the law took effect. We price the barrier with the pool, because on a new build it is never optional.

shortDefinition: A pressure test is the check that proves new gas piping holds without leaking before it goes into service. The plumber caps the system, pumps it up with air, and watches a gauge for a set time. If the reading holds steady, the pipe passes and the inspector signs it off.
definitionHtml:
No gas reaches a new Arizona home until the pipe proves it is tight. The pressure test is how it proves that, and the method is old and simple. Cap every open end, disconnect the piping from the meter or the propane tank, close the appliance valves, and pump the system full of air. Then stand there and watch the gauge. A needle that holds means no leak.

Section G2417 of the 2021 International Residential Code sets the floor. The test pressure runs at least 1.5 times the maximum working pressure and never below 3 psig, whatever the design calls for. The hold is at least 10 minutes. The pressure comes from air, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, or another inert gas, never oxygen, because oxygen meeting a trace of pipe oil is an explosion risk. Leaks get found with soap bubbles or an approved detector, never a flame.

Arizona jurisdictions routinely ask for more than the code floor, so the IRC number alone will not get you signed off. For example, Pinal County requires 10 psi, more than three times the minimum, on a gauge no larger than 30 psi, and the pressure has to hold while the inspector watches for at least 10 minutes. The bulletin also puts the burden on you: the system must already be under test pressure when he arrives, not pumped up after.

The test lands at rough-in, in the same visit as framing, electrical, and plumbing, before drywall closes the walls. That is also the visit where the CSST bonding gets confirmed, so treat gas rough-in as one phase. Passing it is what lets Southwest Gas set your meter and turn on service. Fail it and the code answer is to replace the defective section, not patch it, which is why a bad gas test can push drywall by a week.

shortDefinition: The Residential Contractors' Recovery Fund is an Arizona consumer-protection fund, run by the Registrar of Contractors, that can pay a homeowner harmed by a licensed residential contractor. Licensed contractors pay into it. State law caps payment at $30,000 per claim and $200,000 total against any one license.
definitionHtml:
Arizona keeps a pool of money for homeowners whose licensed builder fails them. Every licensed residential contractor pays an assessment into the Residential Contractors' Recovery Fund, and the Arizona Registrar of Contractors administers it. When a residential contractor's defective work or walk-off leaves you out of pocket and you cannot collect from the contractor, the fund can repay your actual damages.

Two conditions decide most claims. First, A.R.S. 32-1132 limits the fund to people who own the damaged home and occupy it, or intend to, as a primary residence. Individual owners qualify, and so do certain LLCs, revocable living trusts, community associations for common areas, and lessees who contracted directly. A rental you never live in generally does not. Second, the contractor had to be properly licensed when the contract was signed, when you made the first payment, or when the work started. Hire someone unlicensed and no fund exists for you at all.

Then the caps bite. A.R.S. 32-1132.01 sets the maximum individual award at $30,000 and counts only actual damages, meaning the reasonable cost to finish the contract and repair the bad work, less the unpaid contract balance and anything you already recovered elsewhere. A.R.S. 32-1139 caps the fund's total liability at $200,000 for any one contractor's license, paid pro rata once claims run past it.

For example, ten Casa Grande families harmed by the same builder, each with a $30,000 claim, split $200,000 instead of collecting $300,000.

The fund is a different instrument from a contractor's license bond, and homeowners mix the two up constantly. The bond is a surety the contractor buys and posts to hold a license, and a claim runs against that one contractor's bond. The fund is a statewide pool paid for by every licensed residential contractor. On a $1.5 million Rio Verde build, $30,000 is a backstop, not coverage.

shortDefinition: A rough-in inspection is the code check that happens after framing, plumbing, electrical, and mechanical work is in place but before anything covers it. The inspector confirms the hidden work matches the approved plans. Nothing may be insulated, drywalled, or stuccoed until it passes.
definitionHtml:
Every finished wall hides wiring, pipes, ducts, and structural connections. The rough-in inspection is the one visit where an inspector can still see all of it. It lands after the shell is up and the trades have run their systems, and before insulation, drywall, or stucco closes anything in.

Arizona cities describe the timing almost identically. Scottsdale calls its framing inspection for the moment when walls, fire blocking, draft stops, and fireplaces are done and the electrical, plumbing, and mechanical are roughed in, "but before any of this work is covered." Phoenix runs a pre-drywall inspection over the same scope. Some jurisdictions break it into separate rough plumbing, rough electrical, and rough mechanical visits, then follow with framing. The rule underneath does not change: no cover-up before sign-off.

What gets checked is what you can never see again. Stud spacing and headers, hold-downs and shear panels, fire blocking, pipe support and slope, gas and water pressure tests, box fill and wire staples, duct sealing, and roof penetrations.

For example, say a drywall crew boards a 2,400 square foot Apache Junction home before the rough-in passes. The inspector arrives, finds nothing left to look at, and fails it. The crew cuts the board back open at every inspected point, waits for a re-inspection, then patches and re-tapes. That is a week of schedule plus labor nobody budgeted. Scheduling is its own trap: Pinal County gives a same-day visit only if you call the inspection line by 6 am, so a late call parks the next four trades for a day.

A rough-in inspection is not the final inspection. Rough-in checks concealed work in the middle of the build. The final checks the finished house at the end and clears the way for your certificate of occupancy. You pass both, in that order.

shortDefinition: A self-latching gate is a pool gate that latches shut on its own every time it swings closed, with nobody touching it. Arizona law also requires that gate to be self-closing, to open outward away from the pool, and to carry its latch at least 54 inches above the ground.
definitionHtml:
A pool gate does two separate jobs, and people mix up the names. Self-closing means a spring hinge or closer pulls the gate shut with nobody touching it. Self-latching means the latch catches on its own once the gate arrives. A gate that swings shut but does not catch is the most common failure in a pool barrier, because a small child can push it right back open.

A.R.S. 36-1681 gives three legal ways to place the latch. Put it at least 54 inches above the underlying ground. Or put the release on the pool side of the gate, at least 5 inches below the top of the gate, with no opening larger than half an inch within 24 inches of that release. Or secure the gate with a padlock, key, electric opener, or integral combination, in which case the latch can sit at any height. Whichever you pick, the gate has to open outward, away from the pool.

Local rules repeat it. Maricopa County requires gates that are self-closing, self-latching, and open away from the pool, with the latch at 54 inches or greater. Where a house door opens straight onto the pool deck, the county allows an alarm in place of a gate: at least 85 decibels, sounding within 7 seconds of the door opening and running at least 30 seconds.

For example, a Scottsdale build using the block yard wall as its barrier needs hardware on one side gate only. Spring hinges and a gravity latch mounted at 56 inches, swinging away from the water, clears the state rule with margin.

Hardware ages badly, and this is the piece that fails first. Hinges sag, latches drift out of alignment, and a gate that caught at final inspection may not catch a year later. Test it the simple way: swing it wide, let go, and watch it latch by itself.

shortDefinition: A thermal barrier is the fire-rated layer that separates foam plastic insulation from the inside of a house, so the foam cannot ignite during a fire. Half-inch gypsum board is the standard way to build one. Despite the name it controls fire, not heat, which makes it different from a radiant barrier or a vapor barrier.
definitionHtml:
Foam plastic insulation burns fast and throws off thick black smoke, so the code will not let it face a room you live in. Section R316.4 of the International Residential Code requires foam plastic to be separated from the interior of a building by an approved thermal barrier. That means not less than 1/2 inch gypsum wallboard, or a material that passes both the Temperature Transmission Fire Test and the Integrity Fire Test of NFPA 275. Put simply: from inside a finished room, you should not see or touch bare foam.

Attics and crawl spaces get an easier standard. Under Section R316.5.3, where attic access is required and the space is entered only for repairs or maintenance, a lighter ignition barrier can cover the foam instead. Listed options include 1 1/2 inch mineral fiber, 1/4 inch wood structural panels, or 3/8 inch gypsum board. Foam tested for exposed use under Section R316.6 needs no cover.

For example, a Scottsdale home with closed-cell spray foam under the roof deck ends up with a sealed, conditioned attic and no drywall on that slope. It passes because the installer either uses a product with an evaluation report for exposed use or coats the foam with an ignition barrier. The garage is stricter. Foam there sits behind 1/2 inch gypsum board, the full thermal barrier, because a garage is a common place for a fire to start.

Three layers in a house share the word barrier and do unrelated jobs. A thermal barrier is a fire rule. It buys people time to get out before the foam behind it lights. A radiant barrier is reflective attic foil that bounces the sun's radiant heat away from your ceiling. A vapor barrier is a sheet, usually polyethylene under a slab, that blocks moisture moving through an assembly. Fire, heat, water. Only the thermal barrier comes from the fire provisions, and only it is satisfied by drywall.

shortDefinition: UL 9540 is the safety standard for energy storage systems, and the listing a home battery has to carry before a building department will approve it. It covers the whole unit: cells, power conversion, controls, enclosure, and cooling. UL 9540A is a separate fire test method, not a listing.
definitionHtml:
UL 9540 is UL Solutions' Standard for Energy Storage Systems and Equipment. It is a system-level listing, which is the part people miss. A cell can hold its own certification and still leave the finished product unlisted, because UL 9540 judges the assembled unit: cells, power conversion equipment, controls, cooling, and the enclosure it all lives in. A Powerwall or an Enphase battery carries the mark as one product.

Section R328 of the 2021 International Residential Code makes that listing the price of entry: a home battery has to be listed and labeled to UL 9540 before it goes in. From there the section sets sizes. One unit tops out at 20 kWh. The total allowed indoors, in a utility closet, basement, or storage room, is 40 kWh, and a garage, exterior wall, or ground mount allows up to 80 kWh. Units sit at least 3 feet apart.

UL 9540A is a different animal, and conflating the two is the common error. It is a test method, titled Test Method for Evaluating Thermal Runaway Fire Propagation in Battery Energy Storage Systems. Nothing is ever UL 9540A listed, because the test produces a report, not a listing. What that report buys is relief: R328 lets units sit closer than 3 feet, or in larger totals, when the report documents the tighter arrangement is safe.

For example, a Fountain Hills home pairing rooftop solar with two garage-wall batteries clears both caps easily, since a garage allows 80 kWh. Setting them closer than 3 feet is the part that needs paper, and only the maker's UL 9540A report buys it. The other Arizona catch is the code edition. R328 is new in the 2021 IRC and did not exist in the 2018 edition, and Arizona cities are split between the two. In a city still on 2018, the UL 9540 label plus NFPA 855 and the maker's instructions carry the review, so ask your AHJ which edition it enforces before you buy.

shortDefinition: An affidavit of disclosure is a form Arizona law requires from a seller of five or fewer unsubdivided parcels in an unincorporated county area. It must reach the buyer at least seven days before transfer, and the buyer may rescind the sale for five days after receiving it.
definitionHtml:
Buy a raw parcel out in unincorporated county land and you should receive a specific document before closing. It is the affidavit of disclosure, and A.R.S. 33-422 makes it mandatory for "a seller of five or fewer parcels of land, other than subdivided land, in an unincorporated area of a county." Subdivided lots are covered by other rules. This form exists for the parcels that fall outside them.

Two deadlines matter. The seller must furnish the affidavit "at least seven days before the transfer of the property." After you receive it, you get a right to rescind "for a period of five days." That is a short window, so read the form the day it arrives rather than the day before closing.

What makes this worth your attention is the content. The affidavit asks the seller to state the things that quietly decide whether a lot is buildable at all. Is there legal access, or does reaching the parcel mean crossing someone else's land? Are the roads publicly maintained, or will you be grading them yourself? Is there a water supply, and what kind? How will sewage be handled? Are utilities actually at the property, or merely nearby?

Those answers change a budget enormously. A parcel with no legal access needs an easement negotiated before anything else happens. A parcel with no water needs a well, a hauled-water arrangement, or both.

The affidavit is a seller disclosure, not a government certification. Nobody inspects the lot to confirm the answers. Treat it as the starting point for your own diligence rather than the end of it, and verify the access, water, and utility claims independently before the five day window closes.

shortDefinition: Caliche is a layer of desert soil whose particles are cemented together by calcium carbonate, forming a hard, nearly waterproof crust. In Arizona it can sit at or just below the surface and run several feet thick, and it slows excavation for footings, utility trenches, pools, and septic fields.
definitionHtml:
Rain carries dissolved calcium into desert ground. Where it stalls and dries, the calcium carbonate glues the soil grains into a solid mass, and that mass is caliche. University of Arizona Cooperative Extension describes two forms: pale lumps under an inch to several inches across, or a continuous layer a few inches to several feet thick. Some crumbles under a shovel; some is close to rock. Not every desert lot has it.

The cost shows up in excavation. Footings have to reach undisturbed bearing soil, utility trenches have to reach depth, and a pool has to come out of the ground. When a cut hits a hard seam, the crew trades the backhoe bucket for a hoe ram or a rock saw, and the day rate climbs while the schedule slips.

The second problem is water. Solid caliche is nearly impermeable, so irrigation and monsoon runoff perch on top of it instead of draining away. Water stands beside a foundation long after a storm, and a tree planted in a hole that stops at the layer drowns slowly. Extension's fix is blunt: dig through the layer, or cut a narrower hole that pierces it, then check that it drops four inches in four hours.

For example, Maricopa County wants three backhoe-dug test holes at least 12 feet deep on a five-acre Apache Junction parcel before it sets a soil absorption rate for septic. Hit refusal partway down, which caliche will cause, and the county tells you to stop and call. The usable depth shrinks and the drain field gets bigger.

Caliche is not expansive soil, and the two get confused constantly. Expansive clay swells with water and shrinks as it dries, so it moves under a slab. Caliche stays put. It is cemented, which makes it decent to build on and miserable to dig. Your soil report calls out both, and the perc test shows whether a hard layer will drive your septic design.

shortDefinition: Construction valuation is the dollar value a building department assigns to a proposed project in order to calculate the building permit fee. It is not the contract price and not the appraised value of the finished home. Most Arizona jurisdictions derive it from a square-foot cost table tied to occupancy group and construction type.
definitionHtml:
The number a building department cares about is not the number on your contract. Construction valuation is the dollar value a jurisdiction assigns to the work described on a permit application, and it exists to size the permit fee. It is not the contract price, not the lender's as-completed appraisal, and not the county assessor's figure for property tax.

Most departments calculate it themselves from a published table. The International Code Council issues Building Valuation Data twice a year, listing average construction costs per square foot by occupancy group and construction type. A wood-framed house is Group R-3, Type VB. On the February 2024 table that cell reads $165.67 per square foot. The department multiplies the rate by gross floor area, then applies its own fee schedule or permit fee multiplier.

For example, a 3,500-square-foot Type VB home prices out at roughly $580,000 of valuation under that table, whatever the contract says. Maricopa County adds a wrinkle. Its written directive DD-5017-01 still uses the ICC 2003 valuation chart, and staff take the higher of its calculated minimum or the applicant's figure. Understating it on the form does not lower the fee.

Two results surprise buyers. Finish quality barely moves valuation, so the same plan with a $90,000 kitchen and one with builder-grade cabinets carry nearly the same permit fee. And one house draws different fees in different Arizona cities, because each jurisdiction picks its own table edition and multiplier. Scottsdale's published permit fee calculator does not ask for a valuation at all, only permit type and square footage.

Valuation is separate from impact fees, which Arizona calls development fees and charges off an adopted schedule rather than project value. It is also separate from plan review fees, which bill on their own line. Ask the AHJ which valuation table it uses before you budget, because that one choice can move the permit fee by thousands.

shortDefinition: Design-bid-build is the traditional delivery method where an owner hires an architect to finish the drawings, sends that completed plan set to general contractors for competing bids, then signs a separate construction contract with the winner. Design and construction run in sequence under two independent agreements.
definitionHtml:
A.R.S. 34-101 puts it plainly for public work: under design-bid-build "there is a sequential award of two separate contracts. The first contract is for design services. The second contract is for construction." Custom-home buyers follow the same order. Hire a designer, wait for a permit-ready plan set, shop it to builders, then award the job.

The bidding step is the reason owners pick it. Three builders pricing identical drawings hand you three numbers you can lay side by side, and the spread says something real about scope, allowances, and who wants the work. You also choose your architect on design alone. Nothing obligates you to take the low bid.

You pay for that pricing power in coordination. Two contracts mean two schedules, two invoicing cycles, and two parties who report to you rather than to each other. No one has to reconcile the architect's roof detail with the builder's truss layout unless you pay for it. Owners also underestimate the calendar: drawings, engineering, and plan review can run months before a builder is selected.

The sharper exposure sits in the seam between the two contracts. For example, the drawings call out a beam that is undersized for its span. The builder writes a change order for the correction, and the architect answers that the builder should have caught it while bidding. You stand between them holding both invoices. Change orders out of that seam are why the winning bid is a starting number, not a final one.

Whoever wins still has to be licensed. A.R.S. 32-1151 makes it unlawful to act as a contractor in Arizona without a license in good standing, so verify the low bidder before you countersign, not after the permit is pulled. Design-bid-build earns its place when your plans are finished and you want the market to price them. Design-build trades that competitive check for one accountable party and an earlier start.

shortDefinition: Design-build is a project delivery method in which one contract covers both the design of a home and its construction. A single company, or a team led by one, answers for the drawings and the finished house, so the owner deals with one accountable party instead of two separate agreements.
definitionHtml:
Arizona defines the term in statute. A.R.S. 34-101, the definitions section for public construction procurement, describes design-build as a method in which "there is a single contract for design services and construction services." Private custom homes borrow the structure without the public bidding rules. You sign one agreement, and the party behind it owns both the plans and the house.

One contract changes who answers for what. If a window detail leaks, there is no argument over whether the drawing was wrong or the installation was. The same entity is on the hook either way, which is what single point of accountability means. The phases also overlap. The team can price the truss package while interior selections are still open, and grading can start before the last elevation is final. That overlap often pulls weeks off the calendar.

The construction half still needs its own credential. A.R.S. 32-1102 sorts Arizona contractor licenses into classes, among them general residential contracting and general dual licensed contracting. A design firm cannot simply extend its scope into building. Whoever signs must hold, or partner with a holder of, the right ROC class for residential work. Check the contractor's license number on the contract, not the marketing page.

The trade-off is pricing pressure. You choose the builder before finished drawings exist, so there is no plan set to send to three general contractors for competing numbers. You buy on reputation, past work, and a transparent fee. For example, a Fountain Hills owner who hires a design-build team in January gets one contract and an earlier start, and never learns what two other builders would have charged.

Design-build differs from design-bid-build, where an architect finishes the drawings under one agreement and a separate contractor builds them under another. Before signing, ask how the design fee is separated, so you know what you owe if you like the plans but not the price.

shortDefinition: An exempt well is an Arizona well whose pump is rated at no more than 35 gallons per minute and that serves a household rather than irrigation. State law lets it skip the groundwater rights and permits a larger well needs inside an Active Management Area, but you still file a Notice of Intent to Drill.
definitionHtml:
Arizona sorts wells by pump size. A.R.S. 45-402 defines an exempt well as one whose pump has a maximum capacity of not more than thirty-five gallons per minute, used under A.R.S. 45-454, the section on small non-irrigation wells. Fit a bigger pump and it becomes a non-exempt well.

What the exemption is worth depends on where the lot sits. Inside an Active Management Area (AMA), a basin the state manages tightly, pumping from a non-exempt well takes a grandfathered right, a service area right, or a withdrawal permit. An exempt well needs none of them. Outside an AMA, the Arizona Department of Water Resources (ADWR) says wells face fewer requirements to begin with, so the exemption buys less.

Exempt does not mean unregistered. You file Form 55-40, a Notice of Intent to Drill, before any well is drilled, deepened, or modified, and a licensed well-drilling contractor has to do the work. ADWR has 15 days to process the notice under A.R.S. 45-596(D). If the water will serve a home on five acres or fewer, your county health authority reviews the application first.

For example, a buyer on a five-acre Rio Verde Foothills lot files the 55-40 and gets a registered exempt well. None of that guarantees water. ADWR's approval does not override a local ordinance restricting wells, and its well-spacing rules, written to limit drawdown at neighboring wells, skip exempt wells inside an AMA and every well outside one. A legal well can still go dry as the neighbors pump.

That risk is why owners on unincorporated land keep a fallback, usually hauled water into a cistern. An exempt well is a legal status, not a type of hardware. The hole, casing, pump, and tank match any private well. Two identical wells next door can differ only in the pump, and only one is exempt.

shortDefinition: A fixed-price contract, also called a lump-sum or stipulated-sum contract, sets one total price for a defined scope of work before construction starts. The builder carries the risk of cost overruns on that scope. The price still moves for change orders and for allowance items that land above the budgeted number.
definitionHtml:
One number, agreed before the first shovel. That is a fixed-price contract, also written as a lump sum or stipulated sum. You and the builder settle the plans, specs, and scope, and the builder names a total. If framing labor climbs or the lumber package runs over, the builder absorbs it. Buy well and the builder keeps the difference.

That risk transfer is priced in. A builder who cannot pass through overruns carries contingency inside the bid for material swings, weather delays, and the gaps a drawing set never closes. You pay for that cushion whether or not it gets spent, and you never see the line items. Certainty is what you are buying.

A fixed price is fixed against the scope, not against your decisions. Two things still move it. An allowance is a placeholder budget for a selection you have not made yet, say $18,000 for flooring. Choose tile above it and you pay the difference. A change order covers work you add or alter after signing, like adding a casita. A.R.S. 32-1158 requires an Arizona residential contract to state the total dollar amount to be paid, including tax, so paper every change against that total.

For example, a Cave Creek buyer signs a fixed price of $1.2 million on a complete, engineered plan set. Lumber comes in $22,000 over estimate and the builder eats it. The same buyer later upgrades to an RV bay, which is new scope, so a change order lifts the contract to about $1.24 million. Read the exclusions, because many fixed-price contracts carve out unforeseen soil conditions like caliche or rock.

Fixed price fits finished drawings and locked selections, and one stated total is the simplest number to hand a construction lender. Cost-plus runs the other way, billing documented costs plus a fee with the owner carrying the swings. A guaranteed maximum price sits between them, open books under a hard cap.

shortDefinition: A general contractor is the licensed business that holds the prime construction contract and runs the whole build, hiring and paying the subcontractors. Arizona does not license a trade called general contractor. It licenses by classification, and a custom home falls under general residential contracting.
definitionHtml:
A general contractor is the licensed business that signs the prime contract and takes on the whole build. They hold the schedule, pull the permits, hire and pay the subcontractors, and answer to you for the finished house. On a custom home, the general contractor is simply your builder.

Here is the part that surprises people. Arizona does not license a trade called "general contractor." A.R.S. 32-1102 sets out license classifications instead. The one that covers a house is general residential contracting. The statute describes it as work by "any general contractor or subcontractor" who builds, alters, or repairs a residential structure. So the phrase does appear in the law. It just names who does the work, never the license itself.

The real split is between general and specialty. A general residential license lets one firm take on the entire house. A specialty residential license covers a single trade, such as roofing or plumbing. A specialty licensee cannot legally contract for the whole project. The Registrar of Contractors gives each classification a code, and that code prints on the license.

Two things are worth checking before you sign. First, the classification has to match the job. A license in the wrong class cannot legally build your home. Second, look up the qualifying party, the person the license actually rests on. A company name tells you nothing about who holds the qualification.

A general contractor also differs from a construction manager, who advises for a fee and holds no trade contracts. And it differs from an owner-builder, where you take the prime role yourself. That last choice hands you the savings and hands you the liability with it.

shortDefinition: A load-bearing wall carries weight from the roof, the floor, or the walls above it and passes that weight down to a beam, a post, and finally the foundation. A partition wall holds up nothing but itself. Which one you are looking at decides whether a wall can be removed cheaply.
definitionHtml:
Every pound of tile, framing, insulation, and drywall overhead has to reach the ground, and a load-bearing wall is one of the paths it takes. The wall picks up weight from the framing above, carries it down through the studs, routes it around any door or window with a header, and hands it to a footing or a thickened pad in the slab. A partition wall holds up only itself and the drywall screwed to it.

The code treats the two as different animals. IRC Section R602.4 says interior load-bearing walls must be built, framed, and fireblocked the same way exterior walls are. Section R602.5 lets a nonbearing wall use 2x3 studs at 24 inches on center with a single top plate. The difference shows at a framing walk. Full-size studs, doubled top plates, and a post landing under a beam mean the wall carries something.

In Phoenix-metro homes the roof load usually arrives by truss, and a truss spans outside wall to outside wall, so plenty of interior walls carry nothing. Not all of them. A great-room beam, a second floor, or a stepped roof drops weight onto specific interior lines. Scottsdale's submittal guidelines make plans dimension interior bearing footings, coordinate every post between the foundation and roof framing sheets, and add an engineering analysis for any bearing wall over 10 feet tall.

For example, opening a kitchen wall in Scottsdale means an engineered beam sized to the span, posts at both ends, and a pad footing under each post, bearing 18 inches below undisturbed soil under the city's amendment. On a post-tension slab nobody saws that hole until the tendons are located. Then comes a revised structural sheet, a resubmittal, and another inspection.

A load-bearing wall is not a braced wall panel. Bearing walls take gravity pressing down; braced panels take wind pushing sideways. Many walls do both, so ask which walls bear while the framing is open.

shortDefinition: The monsoon is Arizona's summer storm season, running June 15 through September 30. A seasonal wind shift pulls ocean moisture into the state, producing short, violent thunderstorms with blowing dust, downburst winds, and heavy rain. For a build it is the season that tests your grading and every roof flashing.
definitionHtml:
The monsoon is a seasonal shift in wind direction, not a single storm. University of Arizona Cooperative Extension describes a high-pressure zone parking near the Four Corners and spinning clockwise, dragging moisture north from the Pacific and Gulf of Mexico. Arizona State Parks puts the season at June 15 through September 30, and notes July and August bring more than half the precipitation the state sees in a year.

What arrives is not steady rain. A cell builds in the afternoon, collapses, and shoves a wall of wind and dust ahead of it. Maricopa County reports that one to three dust storms reach the Phoenix area in a typical year, lasting minutes to an hour. That dust packs into scuppers, valleys, and gutters. Then rain hits sideways, testing every roof edge, window head, and wall penetration.

Volume is the second problem. Storms drop hard on ground that absorbs almost none of it, so runoff sheets rather than soaks. Maricopa County's warning is blunt: six inches of moving water can knock a person off their feet, and two feet can float a car. That is why finished grade and swales matter more here than the annual rainfall total suggests.

The season also moves your schedule. Grading stops when the subgrade is too wet to compact. Roofing stops mid-storm, and a house that is not dried in stays exposed. Fresh stucco needs to cure without a downpour running down it. For example, a builder starting a Cave Creek home in April aims to finish the pad, drainage, and dry-in before mid-June, then plans July and August as slower months.

One thing owners misread: most days inside the window are dry, so this is not a rainy season the way a Gulf Coast summer is. It is a few violent hours scattered across three and a half months. That makes it a detailing problem. Your drainage plan and your flashing either hold for those hours or they do not.

shortDefinition: A parapet is the part of an exterior wall that continues up past the roof surface. On flat-roof desert homes it hides the roof and its equipment behind a clean edge. Because the wall blocks runoff, the roof has to drain through scuppers or canales instead of over an eave.
definitionHtml:
A parapet is the top of an exterior wall carried up past the roof surface. On a flat or low-slope desert home it does the visual work: ducts, condensers, and solar all disappear behind one straight line. That is why the form runs through so much North Scottsdale and Paradise Valley design, and why the National Park Service describes Pueblo Revival buildings as having "flat roofs with parapeted walls."

Drainage is the trade-off. With a wall in the way, water cannot run off an eave, so the roof must be drained on purpose. Under IRC Section R903.4, unless a roof sheds over its edges, roof drains go at each low point. Water leaves through scuppers, openings cut through the parapet, or canales, the Southwest version that throws water clear of the wall.

Section R903.4.1 adds a backup: where the perimeter rises above the roof so water gets trapped if the primary drains clog, the code requires secondary overflow drains or scuppers. In a monsoon cell that is not paperwork. Blowing dust packs a scupper, rain follows, and a parapet roof becomes a shallow pool held back by wall flashing.

So a parapet is won or lost at the cap and the inside corner. R903.2 requires flashing that keeps moisture out of joints in copings and at parapet wall intersections. R903.3 requires the wall to be capped, or coped, with noncombustible weatherproof material at least as wide as the wall. IIBEC notes the coping should slope back toward the roof so runoff does not stain the wall.

Height is the other decision. A taller parapet screens taller equipment, but it is still wall, so its top usually counts toward measured building height. A parapet is not a fascia and not an eave, which sit at or below the roof plane. For example, settle how tall a Paradise Valley parapet must be to hide rooftop units before elevations get drawn against the height cap.
