shortDefinition: A preliminary twenty day notice is the written notice an Arizona subcontractor or supplier must serve to preserve mechanics' lien rights. It goes out within twenty days of first supplying labor or materials. Receiving one is routine paperwork, not a claim that anything has gone wrong.
definitionHtml:
A few weeks into a build, official-looking letters start arriving. A lumber yard you never hired, a truss plant, a concrete supplier. Each one announces that it has furnished materials to your property. Most owners read the first one and assume something has gone wrong. Almost always, nothing has.

That letter is a preliminary twenty day notice, and A.R.S. 33-992.01 requires it. Anyone who supplies labor, professional services, materials, machinery, fixtures, or tools to your job has to serve one to keep their lien rights alive. The statute says it must be "given not later than twenty days after the claimant has first furnished" those items to the jobsite. Miss the window and the claimant generally loses the right to lien for that work.

The notice goes to several people at once, not just you. The statute directs it to the owner, the original contractor, the construction lender if there is one, and whoever the sender actually contracted with. That is why you receive copies from firms you have no agreement with. They are on your house, so they notify you.

Read it as a signal that the paper trail is working. A supplier who serves notice is following the law. The one worth worrying about is the sub who never sends anything and later claims a lien anyway. What the notice does not tell you is whether that supplier has been paid, so pair it with lien waivers collected at each draw.

A preliminary twenty day notice is not a mechanics' lien, and not a demand for money. It is a placeholder that keeps a future lien possible. The lien itself is a separate recorded document with its own, much later deadline.

shortDefinition: A private well is a water well that serves one home or a few homes, drilled into groundwater on the owner's own land instead of tying into a city main. The owner pays for the drilling, the pump, the power, the testing, and every repair, and no utility monitors the water.
definitionHtml:
A rig bores the hole and sets steel or plastic casing so the walls cannot cave in. A submersible pump hangs below the standing water level. It sends water to a pressure tank near the house, which holds a reserve under air pressure so the pump does not restart every time you open a tap. Arizona requires a licensed well-drilling contractor, and ADWR gives the finished well a registration number that starts with 55.

Depth is the number nobody can quote up front. It follows the basin, and Arizona is a state of basins. ADWR publishes what nearby wells found, through its Wells 55 map and its Groundwater Site Inventory. A careful driller reads those logs for your road before pricing, because drilling and casing sell by the foot. Two lots a mile apart can be a modest well and a punishing one.

The ongoing duty is what buyers underestimate. State health officials put it plainly: private well water is not tested or regulated by any government organization, so the owner is the only one watching. ADHS says to test a new well for arsenic, coliform bacteria, fluoride, lead, nitrates, dissolved solids, and uranium. Then coliform and nitrates yearly, and arsenic, fluoride, and uranium every five years.

For example, a buyer on unincorporated land near Rio Verde Foothills should pull the well log and the last water-level reading before closing, then budget for a pump replacement. A lot with no producing well ends up on trucked hauled water into a cistern instead. If a neighbor offers to share a well, note that ADWR does not regulate shared well agreements and will not step into a dispute.

A private well is the physical system. An exempt well is the legal label the state puts on a small one, based only on the pump rating. Most single-family wells carry both descriptions, so the paperwork question and the water question get answered separately.

shortDefinition: A qualifying party is the individual an Arizona contractor's license actually rests on. State law makes this person responsible for the licensee's conduct under the license, and they must either hold an ownership interest in the license or be regularly employed by the licensee.
definitionHtml:
A company name on a truck tells you very little. Behind every Arizona contractor's license stands a specific person, called the qualifying party. A.R.S. 32-1101 defines that person as one "who is responsible for a licensee's actions and conduct performed under the license." They must also either hold an ownership interest in the license or be regularly employed by the licensee.

The qualifying party is the one who sat the exams and whose experience the Registrar of Contractors accepted. The license belongs to the company, but the competence behind it belongs to that individual. Two firms can hold the same classification and still be very different builders. The classification describes the scope of work allowed. The qualifying party describes who actually knows how to do it.

That gap has a practical consequence. If the qualifying party leaves, the license does not simply roll on without them. The licensee has to replace that person, and the license can go inactive if the gap is not filled. A builder who swapped qualifying parties partway through a project is worth asking about.

Checking is easy. The ROC license search lists the license number, its classification, its status, and the qualifying party by name. Look for a license that has stayed active without breaks, and a qualifying party who has been in place for years rather than months. Then confirm the classification actually covers your work, because a contractor's license in the wrong class cannot legally build your home.

A qualifying party is not the same thing as the license, and not the same as the owner of the business. An owner may hold no personal license at all. So when you vet a builder you are really checking two things at once: that the company holds a current license in the right class, and that a named, experienced person stands behind it.

shortDefinition: A rafter is a single sloped framing member that runs from the ridge at the peak of a roof down to the top of an exterior wall, carrying the roof deck and the roofing above it. Carpenters cut rafters on site, which is why the method is called stick framing or conventional roof framing.
definitionHtml:
A rafter is one board in a roof frame, cut to the plan's pitch and set in place by a carpenter. It runs from the ridge down to the exterior wall's top plate, and the roof sheathing, underlayment, and tile sit on top of it. Framing a roof this way is stick framing, or conventional framing.

Opposing rafters want to spread. Gravity pulls the peak down and the feet kick outward, so something must tie the two sides together. IRC Section R802.5.2 uses the ceiling joists, provided they run parallel to the rafters and sit in the bottom third of the rafter height. Where the joists run the wrong way, add 2x4 rafter ties at most 24 inches on center. Collar ties are separate: 1x4s in the upper third of the attic, up to 4 feet apart. Leave the ties out and the ridge board becomes a designed ridge beam on walls or columns.

The payoff is the space underneath. Rafters leave the volume between them open, so a great room can vault to the ridge and an attic can hold rooms. The Building America Solution Center puts it bluntly: a roof carried by truss framing cannot be used for living space. Rafters can. That volume also suits a conditioned attic, with insulation at the roofline and ducts inside the cooled envelope rather than superheated attic air.

For example, a Rio Verde custom home with a vaulted great room is stick framed over that room while trusses cover the rest. The cost runs the other way: trusses arrive engineered and crane on in a day, while a rafter roof is cut and squared over days by skilled carpenters, every span taken from Section R802.4.1 tables or an engineer.

A truss is a finished assembly; a rafter is one member that works only once tied. Rafter notches and holes follow Section R802.7. Cutting a truss member takes a design professional's approval under Section R802.10.4.

shortDefinition: A ramada is a freestanding, open-sided shade structure with a solid roof carried on posts, the Southwest's oldest answer to desert sun. Arizona owners build them over patios, outdoor kitchens, and pool decks. Whether one needs a building permit turns on its size, its utilities, and whether it touches the house.
definitionHtml:
The structure is older than the Spanish word for it. The National Park Service describes a ramada as a four-legged roofed structure without walls, and the Akimel O'odham and Tohono O'odham built them from a mesquite frame with an ocotillo roof lashed with agave fiber. They called it a wa:ato. The modern version keeps the idea: posts, beams, a roof, no walls.

Three backyard structures get confused constantly. A covered patio attaches to the house and continues its roof line, so it is part of the dwelling. A pergola has an open slatted top that filters sun but passes rain. A ramada stands alone and has a real roof, so it throws full shade and sheds a monsoon downpour. That is why the ramada is what goes over an outdoor kitchen.

The permit question turns on size and utilities. In unincorporated Maricopa County, a single-story, non-habitable accessory structure of 200 square feet or less does not require zoning clearance. Scottsdale draws the same line for a building permit, though Planning Services still reviews placement. Run a circuit for fans and lights, a gas line to a grill, or water to a sink, and the exemption is gone.

Skipping a permit never skips zoning. Setbacks apply either way. Maricopa County keeps a detached accessory structure at least three feet off any side or rear lot line and holds it to 30 percent of a required yard. Scottsdale wants 10 feet between an accessory building and the house. For example, a 16 by 20 foot ramada is 320 square feet, so it needs a permit and eats into your lot coverage cap.

Attaching it changes the classification. Once the roof ties into the wall, most Arizona cities treat it as part of the dwelling and require a permit at any size. Close in the sides and it stops being a ramada, heading toward a room addition or a casita, with foundation, energy, and inspection rules to match.

shortDefinition: Roof underlayment is the water-resistant membrane laid over the roof deck and under the tile, shingle, or panel above it. On an Arizona tile roof the tile sheds water and blocks sun, but the underlayment is what actually keeps rain out, and desert heat ages it out long before the tile.
definitionHtml:
Roof underlayment is the sheet material rolled or stuck onto the roof deck before the tile, shingle, or panel goes on. The 2021 International Residential Code requires it in Section R905.1.1 and names four standards: ASTM D226, D1970, D4869, and D6757. For clay and concrete tile, Section R905.3.3 sends you to that same list.

Here is the part buyers get wrong: concrete tile is the wear surface and sunshade, not the waterproofing. As InterNACHI puts it, most roof coverings "are not waterproof, but water-resistant," and are meant to sit over a membrane. Wind-driven rain blows under and between tiles, and the underlayment carries it to the eave. PNNL's Building America Solution Center lists the common choices under tile: a self-adhered peel-and-stick membrane over the deck, or two layers of No. 30 felt.

Heat shortens its life. Hot, dry climates accelerate the loss of volatiles from bituminous underlayment, so a Phoenix roof bakes the felt brittle while the tile above is still sound. That mismatch produces a repair Arizona owners know: a lift and relay. A roofer pulls and stacks the tile, strips the failed underlayment, lays new, and resets the same tile. You pay for labor and membrane, not a new roof.

Slope changes the spec. Under Section R905.3.2, tile needs a slope of at least 2 1/2 in 12, and from there up to 4 in 12 the code requires double underlayment. Water moves slowly on a shallow pitch and backs up under the tile, so those planes get two layers. For example, a low-pitch entry porch tied into a steeper main roof gets a different build.

Underlayment is the roof's version of the water-resistive barrier in a wall, the hidden layer doing the water control while the visible material takes the weather. When you compare roofing bids, the tile line tells you little. Read the underlayment line, and ask how many layers go down.

shortDefinition: Sheathing is the layer of panels, usually plywood or oriented strand board, nailed over wall studs and roof framing to form a structural skin. It stiffens the frame against wind, carries the roofing and the water-resistive barrier, and is what makes a braced wall panel actually work.
definitionHtml:
Sheathing is the panel layer nailed across the outside of the studs and over the rafters or trusses. The code calls the material a wood structural panel, which means plywood, oriented strand board (OSB), or a composite panel bonded with waterproof resin. It turns a frame of separate sticks into one connected shell.

The structural work happens in the nailing. Studs alone cannot resist racking, the sideways lean a wall takes in a windstorm. APA, the engineered wood trade group, puts it plainly: wall bracing keeps walls square during wind events. Sheathing is how most homes get that bracing. Table R602.10.4 lists Method WSP, wood structural panel, at a 3/8-inch minimum with nails 6 inches apart at panel edges and 12 inches in the field. Nail that pattern and the panel becomes a braced wall panel, the prescriptive path. An engineered shear wall does the same job with a designer's calculations instead of a table.

On Arizona walls, sheathing sits under the water-resistive barrier, which sits under the stucco. Three-coat stucco normally goes over structural sheathing and two layers of Grade D paper. One-coat systems change the stack. Rigid foam goes over the framing, the lath fastens through it, and IRC Section R703.7.3.1 lets a single 60-minute paper replace two layers when foam or a drainage space separates it from the stucco. The Building America Solution Center puts the water control layer behind the foam and over the sheathing, and flashes every window to that layer before the foam goes on.

Foam is insulation, not bracing. For example, on a Cave Creek home with a foam-backed stucco wall, the plans still show wood structural panels at each braced wall line, because foam adds nothing to racking resistance.

Sheathing is not siding and not the barrier. It is the structure under both. Roof sheathing follows Section R803, and that deck is what your tile underlayment fastens to.

shortDefinition: A site plan is the scaled overhead drawing of your lot showing where the house and every other structure sit, how far each one stands from the property lines, and where easements, drainage, driveways, and utilities run. Arizona building departments review it before they will issue a permit.
definitionHtml:
Your floor plan shows the house. The site plan shows the lot, drawn to scale from overhead with the house on it. IRC Section R106.2 requires one with every permit application. It has to give the size and location of new construction, any existing structures, and the distances to the lot lines. Every review discipline reads it, so it is the sheet that stalls a permit.

Maricopa County's checklist shows the real bar. It asks for a north arrow, a vicinity map, a scale bar, the parcel number, and dimensioned property lines. Every structure on the ground gets labeled and measured, fences and propane tanks included. A square-footage table carries the lot coverage math, and overhangs of the first 2 feet from the main building do not count. You show a setback measurement from each structure to each property line, all easements, any wash crossing the parcel, the driveway and its surface material, and the septic tank and disposal field with setbacks to the house, the lot lines, and any well within 100 feet.

Buildable area gets settled here, not in design. On a Scottsdale hillside or Environmentally Sensitive Lands lot, the site plan carries a NAOS dedication. A septic system may not sit inside the NAOS at all. The city's checklist also pins the driveway: 100 feet minimum from the right-of-way line at a street intersection, 25 feet from a side property line, 18 percent maximum slope, and a fire truck turnaround past 200 feet.

For example, a Rio Verde Foothills lot with a wash across one corner can lose its planned pad once the drainage flows and septic setbacks land on the drawing.

A plat is the recorded map that created the lot. The site plan is your house on that lot. Scottsdale rejects incomplete submittals without giving correction comments. That pushes a thin plan to a third round before a permit issues.

shortDefinition: Stucco is a cement-based exterior wall coating, called cement plaster in the building code, applied in coats over metal lath and a water-resistive barrier. Two systems are common on Arizona homes: traditional three-coat stucco, and proprietary one-coat stucco applied over rigid foam board.
definitionHtml:
In the building code, stucco goes by another name: cement plaster. It is a wet mix of cement, sand, and water troweled or sprayed onto a wall in layers, then finished for color and texture. The 2021 International Residential Code covers it in Section R703.7 and ties it to ASTM C926 for the plaster and ASTM C1063 for the lath.

Three-coat stucco is the traditional method. A scratch coat of 3/8 to 1/2 inch goes over metal lath, a brown coat of 3/8 inch levels it, and a finish coat carries the color. Total thickness lands near 7/8 inch and the wall picks up 10 to 12 pounds per square foot. Section R703.7.2 requires at least three coats over lath, and two over masonry.

One-coat stucco is misnamed, since it also takes a finish coat. A proprietary fiber-reinforced base goes on at a minimum of 3/8 inch, often over rigid foam board, not open framing. The code does not write it out, so each brand is approved as an alternative through an ICC-ES report under criteria AC11. The wall ends up thinner and lighter, near 4 to 6 pounds per square foot.

The difference is a real line item. One-coat dominates metro Phoenix production subdivisions because it goes up faster and costs less, while custom work here more often specifies three coats for the added thickness and impact resistance. For example, a Cave Creek home gets scratch and brown coats that cure for days before color goes on. Both systems sit over a water-resistive barrier and stop at a weep screed.

Fine cracks come with the material. Cement plaster shrinks as it cures, so a rigid coating over a moving wood frame shows hairline cracks. Stucco is also not EIFS, a look-alike built from foam board and acrylic rather than cement. Ask which system your bid prices, because the two are not the same wall.

shortDefinition: A kerfed door jamb is a door frame with a narrow slot, or kerf, cut into it. One kind of kerf holds a press-in weatherstrip on an exterior door; another receives the drywall edge so the opening can be finished with no casing trim, a look common in modern Arizona homes.
definitionHtml:
A kerf is the narrow cut a saw blade leaves behind. A kerfed door jamb, or kerf jamb, is a door frame with one or more of those slots milled into it on purpose. The word covers two different jobs, and it helps to know which one someone means.

The first is the weatherstrip kerf. Most exterior doors sold today have a slot running up the jambs and across the head. A compression weatherstrip has a barbed fin along its back that presses into that slot and holds the seal in place without nails or glue. When the strip wears out, you pull it out and press a new one in. Door makers' replacement instructions describe exactly that: clean the jambs, then seat the kerf portion of the new strip into the slot along the header and both sides. In Arizona that seal is what keeps dust and 110-degree air outside, so a torn or flattened strip is worth replacing.

The second is the drywall return kerf. Here the slot is cut into the face of the jamb so the wall's drywall finishing bead tucks into it. The wall then runs straight into the frame with no casing trim around the opening. Door suppliers describe it as a clean, flush finish that removes the need for case moldings, which is why kerf jambs show up in Desert Contemporary and modern homes. The trade-off is precision: the framing, the drywall and the jamb all have to line up, and it costs more than a standard frame with casing.

For example, a Scottsdale home with a minimal interior might use casing-free kerf jambs on every interior door, while its front door uses a standard exterior frame with a weatherstrip kerf. If you want the trim-free look, decide early: it changes how the openings are framed and finished, and it is hard to add later. For more on modern looks, see the Arizona home styles guide.

shortDefinition: A shear wall is a wall built to resist sideways forces from wind and earthquakes, usually wood framing covered in structural sheathing nailed on a set pattern, with hold-downs at the ends. It keeps a house from racking. Steel straps and engineered panels can do the same job where a wall has little solid length.
definitionHtml:
Wind pushing on the side of a house tries to slide the top of each wall sideways relative to the bottom. A shear wall is a wall built to take that push and pass it down to the foundation without leaning, racking or tearing loose. In a wood-framed home it is usually a run of studs covered with structural sheathing such as plywood or OSB, nailed at a tight, specified spacing, with the ends of the wall tied down to the foundation.

Shear walls and braced wall panels do the same job in two ways. The International Residential Code's Section R602.10 gives prescriptive bracing: set lengths and methods a builder can follow without an engineer. When a design goes beyond those tables, such as a wall of glass facing a view, tall walls, or a large open great room, an engineer designs shear walls with calculated nailing, sheathing and hold-downs. Several of the IRC's narrow-wall bracing methods, such as portal frames beside a garage door, also call for hold-downs at the panel ends.

People searching for a strap wall or strap shear wall usually mean one of these narrow-wall solutions: steel strap bracing or strap-style hold-downs that let a short length of wall resist the same force a longer sheathed wall would. Simpson Strong-Tie's testing found that tying down the end posts with hold-downs made walls stiffer and stronger, reaching higher loads with less movement.

For example, a Desert Contemporary home in Cave Creek with sliding glass walls across the back may have very little solid wall on that side. The engineer makes up for it with short, heavily nailed shear walls and hold-downs, or a prefabricated shear panel, at the ends of the glass. That is why the wall plan and the window plan have to be settled together. The full code text is summarized in IRC R602 wall construction and bracing.

shortDefinition: A hold-down is a steel connector that ties the end post of a shear wall or braced panel to the foundation or the floor below, so wind or seismic force cannot lift and tip the wall. It is either cast into the concrete or bolted on after framing.
definitionHtml:
When wind pushes on a wall, the wall wants to do more than slide. It wants to tip over, lifting at one end and pressing down at the other. A hold-down (often written holdown) stops that lift. It is a steel connector that bolts, nails or screws to the end post of a shear wall and anchors it to the foundation or to the framing below.

Simpson Strong-Tie, the largest maker of these connectors, describes the hold-down's job as resisting the overturning caused by sideways loads. Its testing also found that restraining the end posts made the whole wall stiffer and stronger, because the sheathing nails along the edge start doing their full share of the work.

Hold-downs come in two basic types. A strap hold-down is a long steel strap set into the concrete when the slab or stem wall is poured, then nailed to the post after framing. A post-installed hold-down is a heavier bracket fastened to the post and to an anchor bolt that was cast into the concrete. Either way, the location has to be known before the pour, so hold-downs are drawn on the foundation plan and checked at the foundation and framing inspections. The International Residential Code calls for them on several of its narrow-wall bracing methods, such as portal frames beside garage doors.

For example, a two-story custom home in Scottsdale with a wide garage door may need strap hold-downs at both sides of the opening. If the strap is missed at the pour, the fix is an engineered retrofit anchor drilled into the concrete, which costs time and an engineer's sign-off. For the code background, see IRC R602 wall construction and bracing and the glossary entry for a braced wall panel.

shortDefinition: An under-cabinet outlet is a receptacle or listed power strip mounted under the upper cabinets so the backsplash stays clear. It must sit no more than 20 inches above the counter, keep every point of the counter within 24 inches of an outlet, and be GFCI protected like any kitchen counter outlet.
definitionHtml:
An under-cabinet outlet is an electrical receptacle mounted on the underside of the upper cabinets, or on the wall just beneath them, instead of in the backsplash. It can be a single receptacle, a row of them, or a continuous power strip (often called plugmold) that runs the length of the cabinet. The point is a clean backsplash: tile or stone slab runs uninterrupted, and the plugs sit out of sight above the counter.

Under-cabinet outlets still have to meet the counter rules in the International Residential Code, Section E3901.4, which follows the National Electrical Code's Section 210.52(C). Along a counter, no point can be more than 24 inches from an outlet, and every counter space 12 inches wide or wider needs one. The outlets must sit on or above the counter and no more than 20 inches above it. Upper cabinets usually hang about 18 inches above the counter, so receptacles on their underside land inside that limit and count toward the required spacing. Outlets hidden behind a built-in appliance or inside an appliance garage do not count. A power strip has to be a product listed for the way it is installed, not a household extension strip screwed to a cabinet. The full placement rules are summarized in IRC E3901 receptacle placement.

Every kitchen counter outlet also needs shock protection. That usually means a GFCI breaker at the panel or a GFCI device upstream, because a reset button under a cabinet is hard to reach and easy to forget. The rules for which outlets need GFCI and AFCI protection, and how they differ by the code edition your city enforces, are in IRC E3902 GFCI and AFCI protection.

For example, a Scottsdale kitchen with a full-height quartzite backsplash might put a power strip under every run of upper cabinets and keep the backsplash bare. An island has no cabinet above it, so its outlets go in a listed pop-up unit in the counter or, where the code allows, on the side of the island just below the counter edge. Because the strip, the backsplash material and the cabinet bottoms all have to line up, this is decided before the electrician roughs in the boxes, not after the tile is set. See the rough-in inspection for when that wiring is checked.
